key_terms.meaning: Short period after the spark, about 0.001–0.002 s, in which the flame nucleus grows before a visible flame front forms.
Stage in which the flame front travels through the unburnt charge and burns it layer by layer.
Final SI stage where leftover unburnt mixture and CO burn during expansion, giving a slow tail of heat release.
Speed of the flame front relative to the unburnt gas ahead of it, measured in m/s.
dp/dθ, the change in cylinder pressure in bar per degree of crank rotation; a smooth SI cycle stays near 1–2 bar/°CA.
Abnormal SI combustion in which the end gas autoignites after the spark and burns very fast, giving a sharp pressure pulse.
Ignition of the charge before the spark arrives, started by a hot spot such as a glowing plug tip or carbon deposit.
Severe knock in which the autoignited end gas burns as a shock-driven wave, giving an extremely high pressure rise.
The last part of the charge to burn; the expanding flame front compresses it, raising its temperature and pressure until it can self-ignite.
In a CI engine, the time from start of injection to the start of detectable heat release, given in ms or °CA.
Rapid CI burning of the fuel that had already mixed with air during the ignition delay.
CI burning phase whose rate is set by how quickly fuel vapour and air can mix, not by chemical kinetics.
Knocking in a CI engine caused by a long delay that lets fuel pile up and then burn too fast in the premixed phase.
Organised rotation of the whole charge about the cylinder axis, used to carry fuel spray around the chamber.
Radial inward flow near TDC, produced as the piston squeezes charge out of the narrow gap between piston crown and head.
Organised rotation of the charge about an axis perpendicular to the cylinder axis, which breaks up into turbulence near TDC.
Swirl angular speed divided by engine angular speed; both in the same units, so it is dimensionless.
Diesel fuel is injected straight into a bowl in the piston crown inside the main cylinder.
Diesel fuel is injected into a small pre-chamber or swirl chamber joined to the main chamber by a throat.
Ratio of cylinder volume at BDC to volume at TDC, written r = V₁/V₂; higher r raises thermal efficiency and knock tendency.

takeaways: SI combustion runs through ignition lag, flame propagation and afterburning, and only the middle stage is fast enough to matter for pressure rise.
Flame speed controls how fast the charge burns; mass burning rate controls how fast pressure rises, and the two are linked but not identical.
Knock starts after the spark in the end gas, pre-ignition starts before the spark at a hot spot, and detonation is knock severe enough to send pressure waves through the chamber.
Knock depends on fuel, engine design and operating conditions together, so any single change can help or hurt depending on the others.
CI combustion has four stages, and the ignition delay at the start decides how much fuel burns in the violent premixed phase.
Diesel knock is cured by shortening the delay or cutting the fuel that accumulates during it, using cetane number, intake temperature, injection timing and chamber design.
Swirl, squish and tumble are ordered air motions that break into turbulence at TDC and decide how well fuel and air mix in both engine types.
A good combustion chamber mixes the charge, burns it quickly, breathes well and keeps hot spots away; SI and CI engines meet these goals with quite different shapes.
bank_note: Long answers here are expected to carry a labelled p–θ diagram of the appropriate stages, then connect knock, delay period and chamber shape into one argument, so practise drawing the diagrams and listing factors in the same answer.

bank.q: Describe the three stages of combustion in an SI engine, and explain with a pressure–crank angle diagram why the flame propagation stage dominates the pressure rise.
outline: Name ignition lag, flame propagation, afterburning with typical durations
Sketch p–θ diagram, mark spark point and peak pressure point
Ignition lag is small, only a flame nucleus grows
Flame propagation burns the bulk of the charge and gives the steep pressure rise
Afterburning gives a slow tail near the end of expansion

bank.q: Define flame speed and flame velocity. Explain how the mass burning rate and the rate of pressure rise are related to them.
outline: Flame speed relative to the unburnt gas; flame velocity in the laboratory frame
Mass burning rate = flame speed × flame front area × unburnt gas density
Rate of pressure rise dp/dθ from first-law analysis of the burnt mass
Effect of flame front area growth and piston motion on pressure rise
Typical smooth SI value of dp/dθ

bank.q: Distinguish clearly between knock, detonation and pre-ignition in an SI engine, stating the origin and the time of each.
outline: Knock begins after the spark and needs an end gas that autoignites
Pre-ignition begins before the spark, triggered by a hot spot
Detonation is severe knock with shock-driven burning and pressure waves
Typical cylinder pressure traces for each
Pre-ignition can lead to knock and knock can overheat surfaces, so the two feed each other

bank.q: Explain the four stages of combustion in a CI engine and mark them on a heat release rate diagram.
outline: Ignition delay from start of injection to start of heat release
Premixed combustion spike from fuel mixed during the delay
Mixing-controlled combustion with a diffusion flame at the spray boundary
Late burning of the tail of fuel
Sketch of heat release rate against crank angle

bank.q: Explain swirl, squish and tumble with neat sketches, and give one advantage of each in an engine.
outline: Swirl: rotation about the cylinder axis, formed by port geometry or a masked inlet valve
Squish: radial flow as the piston squeezes charge from the squish band near TDC
Tumble: rotation about an axis perpendicular to the cylinder axis
Swirl carries spray around the chamber; squish generates turbulence at TDC; tumble breaks up into turbulence at TDC
Definitions of swirl ratio and typical values

bank.q: List the design objectives of a combustion chamber and compare hemispherical and bathtub SI chambers against those objectives.
outline: Objectives: good breathing, good mixing, fast burn, no hot spots, low heat loss, high compression ratio possible
Hemispherical: central plug, short flame travel, good breathing with large valves, but two valves limit layout
Bathtub: cheap, simple, good turbulence, but longer flame travel and lower compression ratio

bank.q: An SI engine knocks after a tune-up that raised compression ratio and advanced the spark. Using the factors affecting knock, explain what happened and suggest four corrective steps.
outline: Higher compression ratio raises end gas temperature and pressure
Advanced spark gives the end gas more time at high pressure
Correctives: retard spark, lower compression ratio, use higher octane fuel, cool the intake charge, reduce deposit-forming richness, redesign chamber to shorten flame travel
Explain each corrective in terms of end gas temperature or reaction time

bank.q: A diesel engine shows a sharp premixed heat release spike and audible knock. Describe five methods of controlling diesel knock and explain how each works.
outline: Use higher cetane fuel to shorten the delay
Advance injection timing or use pilot injection to cut fuel accumulation
Raise intake air temperature and compression ratio to shorten delay
Increase air motion so mixing during the delay improves
Re-entrant bowl or IDI chamber to limit premixed burn
Smaller ignition delay means less fuel ready to burn at once

bank.q: Compare a DI and an IDI diesel combustion chamber for a small tractor engine and a large truck engine, and justify your choice on heat loss, mixing, cost and fuel quality tolerance.
outline: DI: high efficiency, low heat loss, needs high injection pressure and good fuel
IDI: strong swirl in pre-chamber, faster mixing, tolerates poorer fuel, lower efficiency due to throat and heat loss
Truck: DI for fuel economy and power
Tractor: IDI simple, quieter, cheaper, tolerates fuel quality
Mention injection location and spray in each

bank.q: For an SI engine, explain how increasing flame speed changes the rate of pressure rise and the tendency to knock.
outline: Faster flame speed burns the charge earlier and shortens the time the end gas spends at high pressure
Steeper dp/dθ and peak pressure closer to TDC
Less time for pre-flame reactions in the end gas, so knock tendency falls
Ways to raise flame speed: turbulence, short flame travel, central plug, richer mixture
Trade-off: very fast burn raises mechanical loading and NOx

bank.q: Compare ignition lag in an SI engine with ignition delay in a CI engine, and explain how each is linked to knocking in its own engine.
outline: SI lag: chemical and physical, ends when flame nucleus forms; long lag gives more end gas reaction time
CI delay: physical atomisation and vaporisation plus chemical pre-flame reactions
SI long lag is only mildly important because the spark is fixed, but retarded spark increases knock
CI long delay causes fuel accumulation and violent premixed burn
Both are shortened by higher charge temperature and pressure
Conclusion: in SI the end gas time scale matters, in CI the accumulated fuel mass matters

bank.q: Examine the statement: 'A long ignition delay is the only cause of diesel knock.' Support or refute it with reference to chamber design and operating conditions.
outline: Delay is the main cause, but rate of pressure rise depends also on fuel quantity in the delay and on mixing
Poor air motion increases the accumulated fuel
Low compression ratio, cold starting, light load all lengthen delay
IDI chamber geometry and injection characteristics change the premixed spike
Verdict: delay is dominant but not the only factor

bank.q: Evaluate the conflicting demands in combustion chamber design for SI engines and judge which objectives you would relax first in a low-cost small car engine.
outline: Good breathing versus high compression ratio versus short flame travel
No hot spots versus low cost of manufacture
Low heat loss versus fast burn
Relax low heat loss or use a simple bathtub shape, keeping detonation control through spark timing and fuel quality
Justify with efficiency, knock limit and emission trade-offs

bank.q: Assess how swirl, squish and tumble each affect delay period, rate of pressure rise and emissions in SI and CI engines, and state the limits of increasing them.
outline: Swirl and squish raise turbulence, shorten delay, speed up burning
Higher turbulence increases heat transfer and reduces volumetric efficiency
Excessive swirl causes spray impingement and higher NOx
Squish limited by clearance and by tendency to increase heat loss
Trade-off between fast mixing and pumping or heat-loss penalties

glossary.def: Spontaneous ignition of a fuel–air mixture when its temperature reaches the point where the pre-flame reactions run away on their own.
Mass of air supplied divided by mass of fuel supplied in the charge; petrol engines run near 14.7:1 at stoichiometric.
Random, small-scale, swirling motion of the gas that wrinkles the flame front and speeds up burning.
The CI ignition delay measured in crank angle degrees or milliseconds, ending when the first detectable heat release appears.
The thin moving zone where the reaction is taking place and that separates burnt products from unburnt charge.
Rate at which chemical energy of the fuel is set free in the cylinder, usually plotted against crank angle.
Crank angle at which the spark occurs, usually expressed as degrees before top dead centre.
Measure of a petrol's resistance to knock, compared with iso-octane as 100 and n-heptane as 0.
Measure of a diesel fuel's ease of self-ignition; a higher cetane number means a shorter ignition delay.
The narrow gap between the piston crown and the cylinder head at TDC, from which charge is squeezed inward.
A small auxiliary chamber used in IDI engines, connected to the main chamber by a narrow throat.
The recess in the piston crown of a DI diesel engine in which fuel is injected and mixing takes place.
The internal diameter of the engine cylinder, in mm.
Mass of air actually drawn in per cycle divided by the mass that would fill the swept volume at ambient conditions.
A low-temperature combustion concept in which a pre-mixed lean charge ignites by compression at many points at once.
Describing the highest compression ratio or spark advance an engine can use before knock sets in.
Degrees by which the spark or injection is set before top dead centre.
The maximum cylinder pressure in the cycle, usually in bar, and the crank angle at which it occurs.
The volume on an engine test bed that smooths intake pulsations so the airflow measurement is steady.
Running an SI engine with excess air to raise efficiency and reduce knock, at the cost of ignition stability.
Using an exhaust-driven turbine to compress the intake air and pack more mass into the cylinder.
Removal of heat from the cylinder walls, head and piston by water or air so that hot spots and pre-ignition are avoided.
